title: Taiwan Semiconductor Sales Jump 60% In October As AI Boom Continues - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Futures Rise As CoreWeave Jumps, Lifts AI Stocks Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) on Tuesday reported that its October sales surged 59.7% year over year in local currency as it continues to benefit from strong AI chip production. TSM stock rose on the news. The world's largest contract chip manufacturer, better known as TSMC, reported monthly sales of 586.89 billion New Taiwan dollars ($17.85 billion). Its sales increased 14.7% from September. TSMC's October sales put it ahead of pace for the fourth quarter, according to FactSet estimates. On the stock market today, TSM stock rose 2% to close at 396.48. On Monday, it surged 3.5% to close at 388.62 amid a broad rally for chip stocks. However, TSM stock is still below its key moving averages and far below its all-time high of 487.47, reached on Oct. 5. On Oct. 6, TSM stock began a steep drop along with other chip stocks on the Philadelphia semiconductor index, known as SOX. On Oct. 15, Taiwan Semiconductor delivered a beat-and-raise third-quarter report. But TSM stock fell after the report. TSMC makes chips for a host of fabless chip designers including AMD (AMD), Apple (AAPL) and Nvidia (NVDA). Lately it has benefitted from high demand for chips for data centers running artificial intelligence applications. "October's sales again set a new monthly record, and the step up from September gives TSMC a strong start to the December quarter," Wedbush Securities analyst Matt Bryson said in a report. Wedbush has reiterated its 'outperform' rating and NT$3,300 price target on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (ADR) (NYSE:TSM), after October sales exceeded seasonal expectations. Revenue of the Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer increased 14.7% month on month to a record NT$586.89 billion, representing growth of 59.7% year on year and a strong start to the December quarter. Sales in the first 10 months of 2026 reached NT$4.49 trillion, up 43.3% compared with the same period last year. Wedbush expects TSMC to deliver approximately 13% sequential revenue growth in the fourth quarter, with October already accounting for around 35% of its NT$1.695 trillion forecast. That compares with October's average contribution of approximately 34% to quarterly revenue over the past five years, suggesting the company is running slightly ahead of normal seasonal trends. The broker's positive investment thesis remains unchanged, supported by strong demand expectations, constrained component supplies and continued confidence among TSMC's customers. Recent supply-chain discussions, including conversations involving customers such as AMD, point to solid demand expectations through the December quarter and into 2027. Wedbush also highlighted favourable foreign exchange movements, with the Taiwanese dollar averaging 32.2 against the US dollar in October, compared with TSMC's fourth-quarter planning assumption of 31.8. The currency had subsequently weakened to 32.8 against the US dollar, potentially providing additional support for profitability if those levels persist. Wedbush estimates that every 1% movement in exchange rates affects TSMC's gross margins by approximately 0.4%. The broker's NT$3,300 price target is based on approximately 22 times its estimated 2027 earnings per share, adjusted for net cash. title: TSM Stock: October Revenue Up 59.7%, Ahead of Q4 Pace - FinanceFeeds
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) reported record monthly revenue of NT$586.89 billion, approximately $17.88 billion at the exchange rate cited by InvestingCube, for October 2026. The result represents a 59.7% increase from a year earlier and a 14.7% rise from September, providing fresh evidence of strong semiconductor demand following last week’s sharp selloff in AI-related stocks. TSM stock traded at $394.19, up 1.43%, at 11:22 a.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, according to ChartExchange. The American depositary receipts had closed Monday at $388.62, gaining 3.51%, after a particularly volatile week that included a 10.78% decline on November 5. The October revenue figure is the first monthly reading for TSMC’s fourth quarter, which runs through December. It puts the company ahead of the average monthly revenue pace implied by its October 15 guidance of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The result is also relevant to investors watching Nvidia, which reports quarterly earnings on November 17. In its November 10 revenue announcement, TSMC reported October consolidated sales of NT$586.89 billion, compared with NT$511.86 billion in September and NT$367.47 billion in October 2025. The increase of approximately NT$75 billion from September pushed monthly revenue above the previous record of NT$514.81 billion set in August. October was also the first month in which TSMC generated more than NT$580 billion in sales. For January through October, consolidated revenue reached NT$4,485.62 billion, increasing 43.3% from NT$3,130.44 billion during the corresponding period in 2025. October’s 59.7% annual growth exceeded the 43.3% growth recorded over the first ten months. The acceleration is consistent with the company’s previous commentary about strong demand for leading-edge manufacturing, although the monthly release does not identify how much revenue came specifically from AI processors, smartphone chips or other products. The sequential increase is particularly notable because September had already remained close to August’s record. FinanceFeeds previously reported that TSMC’s September revenue reached NT$511.9 billion, up 54.6% year over year, leaving the company operating near its highest recorded monthly sales level. October’s result moves substantially beyond that level, suggesting that the fourth quarter has begun with stronger revenue momentum than the preceding quarter’s final month. The latest revenue number can be compared directly with the outlook management provided during its October 15 earnings announcement. In its third-quarter earnings release, TSMC projected fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, based on an exchange-rate assumption of NT$31.8 per US dollar. That guidance translates to approximately NT$1.663 trillion to NT$1.727 trillion. After October’s NT$586.89 billion, TSMC would need combined revenue of approximately NT$1.076 trillion to NT$1.140 trillion across November and December to reach the original target range. That works out to an average of roughly NT$538.1 billion to NT$569.9 billion per month over the remaining two months. October exceeded even the upper-end monthly requirement by approximately NT$17 billion. If November and December each matched October’s revenue, fourth-quarter sales would reach approximately NT$1.761 trillion, above the New Taiwan dollar equivalent of the company’s original guidance ceiling. This is a comparison using TSMC’s assumed guidance exchange rate, not a revised forecast or a confirmed earnings beat. Actual reported dollar revenue will depend on the company’s financial reporting and exchange-rate treatment during the quarter. October’s roughly $17.88 billion equivalent, calculated using a different exchange rate, should not be mixed directly with the guidance conversion. The company also forecast fourth-quarter gross margin of 65% to 67% and operating margin of 56.5% to 58.5%. Revenue alone cannot establish whether TSMC will meet those profitability targets, especially as it expands advanced manufacturing capacity. FinanceFeeds’ October 15 analysis of TSMC’s third-quarter results examined the company’s $46.72 billion quarterly revenue, 66.4% gross margin and outlook for accelerating sales. TSMC’s October figures arrive after a difficult period for semiconductor stocks. Its US-listed shares fell 10.78% on November 5, closing at $353.10, before recovering 6.33% on Friday and another 3.51% on Monday. The rebound followed concerns about AI infrastructure investment, capital spending and potential delays in data center development. Those concerns had weighed on several companies involved in advanced computing, even as their reported financial performance remained strong. TSMC’s monthly sales figures provide a more direct indication of manufacturing activity. The company produces advanced processors for customers including Nvidia, AMD and Apple, while also supplying chips for custom AI accelerators and other high-performance computing applications. Its third-quarter technology mix showed the growing importance of advanced production nodes. Chips manufactured using 2-nanometer technology accounted for 8% of wafer revenue, while 3-nanometer and 5-nanometer processes contributed 33% and 28%, respectively. Technologies at 7 nanometers and below accounted for 79% of total wafer revenue. TSMC CFO Wendell Huang said during the October earnings announcement that fourth-quarter performance would benefit from continued demand for leading-edge technologies, including the rapid expansion of 2-nanometer production. However, stronger manufacturing revenue does not necessarily establish that every AI customer is increasing its orders at the same rate. TSMC’s monthly report does not disclose customer-level sales, shipment volumes by technology or the contribution of changes in pricing. Profitability also remains a consideration. Management has previously identified margin pressure associated with the introduction of 2-nanometer technology and the higher operating costs of overseas manufacturing facilities. Investors will need the full quarterly results to determine how much of the additional revenue translates into profit. TSMC’s October revenue announcement comes one week before Nvidia’s next earnings report, making the manufacturing data particularly relevant to expectations for the AI accelerator market. Nvidia confirmed that it will release its fiscal third-quarter 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, with an earnings conference call at 5 p.m. ET. The reporting period ended October 25. TSMC’s results provide evidence that demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing remained strong in October, but they cannot independently predict Nvidia’s revenue or earnings. The companies operate at different points in the supply chain, and manufacturing revenue does not necessarily correspond to sales recognized by Nvidia during the same reporting period. Investors will be watching Nvidia’s data center revenue, its forward guidance and management’s comments on accelerator demand, production capacity and customer spending. Those disclosures should offer another perspective on whether the industry’s strong manufacturing activity is continuing to translate into revenue growth for chip designers. For TSM stock, the next milestone will be the November revenue release, which will show whether October’s record was sustainable. November and December need to average approximately NT$570 billion to reach the upper end of the company’s existing fourth-quarter revenue target under its original exchange-rate assumption. October’s NT$586.89 billion provides a strong start and reduces the monthly revenue pace required for the remainder of the quarter. The remaining questions concern whether manufacturing demand can sustain that level and whether TSMC can preserve its projected margins while expanding its most advanced production technologies. Intel Corporation INTC and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company TSM are two premier semiconductor manufacturers competing in advanced chip fabrication and foundry services. Both are competing hard in the AI-powered chipmaking market, with Intel expanding its foundry business and TSM dominating the contract chipmaking market.Intel is currently focusing on AI chips for data centers and PCs, which marks one of the largest architectural shifts for the company in 40 years. The decision is primarily aimed at gaining a firmer footing in the expansive AI sector, spanning cloud and enterprise servers to networks, volume clients and ubiquitous edge environments, in tune with the evolving market dynamics. The foundry operating model is a key component of the company's strategy and is designed to reshape operational dynamics and drive greater transparency, accountability and focus on costs and efficiency. TSM is benefiting from accelerating AI investments, growing demand for advanced semiconductor technologies and aggressive global manufacturing expansion. The company's technological leadership, strong profitability and robust demand outlook position it favorably for sustained growth.Let us try to analyze some of the competitive strengths and weaknesses of the companies to understand who is in a better position to maximize gains from the emerging market trends. Intel is witnessing healthy traction in AI PCs that have taken the market by storm. Its innovative AI solutions are set to benefit the broader semiconductor ecosystem by driving down costs, improving performance and fostering an open, scalable AI environment. The proliferation of generative AI applications is driving significant investments in data center infrastructure. Although GPUs remain at the center of AI computing, CPUs continue to play an important role in supporting AI workloads. This is creating incremental opportunities for Intel's Xeon portfolio. The momentum is encouraging as AI-related infrastructure spending is likely to remain healthy, providing Intel with an opportunity to capitalize on rising compute requirements. Intel is ramping Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake products based on its advanced 18A process technology. Increasing adoption of these products, coupled with an eventual enterprise PC refresh cycle, should support the client business over the long run. The company is also expanding its presence in edge computing and physical AI applications, including robotics. These emerging markets could broaden Intel's addressable opportunity beyond traditional PCs. However, Intel derives a significant part of its revenues from China. As Washington tightens restrictions on high-tech exports to China, Beijing has intensified its push for self-sufficiency in critical industries. This shift poses a dual challenge for Intel, as it faces potential market restrictions and increased competition from domestic chipmakers. The company is also lagging in the GPU and AI front compared to peers, such as NVIDIA Corporation NVDA and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. AMD. Leading technology companies are reportedly piling up NVIDIA's GPUs to build computing clusters for their AI work, driving exponential revenue growth. TSM remains a key beneficiary of accelerating investments in AI infrastructure. Growing demand for AI accelerators, custom chips, networking processors and agentic AI applications is driving the adoption of its advanced manufacturing technologies. TSM's leadership in cutting-edge semiconductor manufacturing provides a significant competitive advantage. Management expects N2-family annual capacity to more than double in 2027, supported by robust smartphone and HPC/AI demand. Its next-generation A14 technology remains on track for risk production in 2027 and volume production in 2028, strengthening long-term growth opportunities. TSM is accelerating manufacturing investments to capitalize on sustained semiconductor demand. The company reiterated its 2026 capital expenditure budget of $60-$64 billion and expects investments during 2026-2028 to significantly exceed those of the preceding three years. The company is developing nearly 20 fabrication facilities globally. Its second Arizona fab is scheduled to begin volume production in the third quarter of 2027, while an additional 3-nanometer capacity in Taiwan is expected to become operational during 2027 and 2028. These investments should strengthen supply capabilities and support future revenue growth.However, TSM faces headwinds from rising manufacturing costs, significant capital expenditure requirements and ongoing global capacity expansion. The expansion of overseas manufacturing facilities, particularly in the United States, is expected to increase gross margin dilution to 3-4 percentage points over the next few years, compared with approximately 2 percentage points anticipated for 2026. Elevated spending could constrain free cash flow generation and weigh on returns if demand growth fails to keep pace with capacity additions. Moreover, rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties are pressuring consumer-oriented and price-sensitive end markets, prompting management to adopt a cautious approach toward 2027 business planning. These factors could limit near-term margin expansion and profitability despite robust demand for advanced semiconductor technologies. title: Why Is TSM Stock Rising Overnight? - TradingView
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) shares rose 1% in overnight trading ahead of Tuesday after the Taiwanese contract chipmaker reported a sharp increase in monthly sales. Gains were tempered by controversy surrounding Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a report speculating that the AI chipmaker is slowing chip orders. The go-to chipmaker for Nvidia and Apple (AAPL) said its October revenue rose 60% to NT$586.9 billion ($17.9 billion). That compares to the 51% growth pace in September quarter and 63% growth analysts polled by Bloomberg expect in the current quarter. Although TSMC’s upbeat monthly update is a bullish signal for the chip trader, semiconductor stocks were mixed in early Tuesday hours. NVDA shares were 1% higher after a sharp slide on Monday, while Intel (INTC) was up 0.3% and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) was down 0.4%. Nvidia is said to be considering slowing chip orders, which would affect upstream supply chain players like TSMC and ASE Technology Holding, a Taiwanese chip assembly and packaging firm, according to a report in the Taiwanese outlet Commercial Times. AMD could be a potential beneficiary. The developments come amid a volatile period of chip stocks. Last week, TSM fell sharply in tandem with other semiconductor stocks after Democrats, seen to be pro-regulation for AI and data centers, won both the Senate and House in the midterm elections. TSM stock is now down about 20% from its peak in early October. Nvidia CEO Huang on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a person U.S. authorities suspect to be a Chinese spy. The admission has created a financial shock, with investors panicking that Huang, a key force behind the AI boom, might lose his CEO title. On Monday, a law firm filed a class action lawsuit against Nvidia and Huang for misleading investors and Delaware senator Chris Coons called for a congressional investigation on national security grounds. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for TSM remained ‘neutral’ for a second day. “$TSM Oct monthly rev drove past expectations. Set a new Oct record $SOXX $SOXL,” a trader wrote. On the news report regarding slowing orders, a trader wrote: Nvidia may cut its H200 chip orders at $TSM due to the Jensen scandal. H200's primarily go to China. title: My Son's First Buck Hunt Gave Me a Memory I'll Never Forget - 97.9 WGRD
content: If you're a deer hunter, you never forget the feeling of harvesting your first deer. Watching my son experience the excitement of harvesting his first buck with a bow is a memory we'll cherish for the rest of our lives. My son's first word wasn't Mom or Dad. It was "Buck." I used to hold him up in front of one of my deer mounts, point to it, say 'buck,' and let him reach out and touch it. Then one day, he said it himself. From that moment on, I knew something special was beginning. Passing along what I've learned and sharing my passion with the next generation has turned into an incredible journey that we'll cherish forever. I remember getting Evan his first bow and setting up a little shooting range in our old barn. I also remember the times he'd sit in the blind with me, watching deer and taking in all the amazing things Mother Nature had to offer. Long before he was old enough to sit in a stand on his own, he was already learning, observing, and sharing those special moments with me. It's been such a blessing to share these experiences with Evan and his brother and watch them grow into the fine young outdoorsmen they are today. This past weekend, it all came full circle for the three of us when Evan harvested his very first buck with his bow. It's a moment we'll never forget and one that makes all those years of memories together even more special. It's pretty special to see all that practice finally pay off. My favorite time of year is always from Halloween until the day before gun season. The deer are moving, and those big bucks we've been watching on our trail cameras start showing up. There's just something about this time of year that makes it so special. Evan's big brother, Isaak, spotted the buck coming into the field and watched as it walked straight toward his little brother. Evan didn't even realize the buck was there until it approached and started feeding in the food plot. Evan said, "My legs started shaking, my arms were shaking, and I could barely lift my bow. Then, just like that, one, two, three seconds later, I let my arrow fly. I couldn't believe how fast it all happened!" Isaak said he heard the shot, followed by the crash, and immediately made his way over to see what had happened. He said, "Evan couldn't even get any words out. He was just holding his hands up, saying, 'Big buck!'" I heard the shot too, but I was surrounded by deer and couldn't move. Once the area cleared, I made my way down to the boys, only to find out they had already tracked the deer themselves, something I've spent years teaching both of them. Inside, I was pretty choked up inside, but I had to play it cool and let the boys tell me everything that had just happened. It was one of those moments I'll never forget. This was a Hall of Fame weekend for the boys and me. I couldn't be prouder of both of them for their hard work, patience, and willingness to wait for the right deer. These are the kinds of memories the three of us will be talking about for the rest of our lives. It doesn't get any better than this, and it doesn't get much more "Pure Michigan" than that! Now it's Isaak's and my turn to hopefully get our chance at bringing home a big buck or doe. title: TSM Stock at 21x After a 30% Chip Sell-Off [2026] - shattered.io
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the company behind the NYSE ticker TSM, is the stock a Motley Fool columnist would buy and hold after a brutal stretch for chip shares. In a column syndicated on Yahoo Finance and headlined “Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I’d Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever.”, the author argues that TSM stock offers a better deal than the two names that dominated the AI trade. Listings show the piece ran on November 7, 2026. The timing matters. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index sits roughly 30% below where it stood on October 6, Nvidia is down 21%, and Micron is down 34%. TSMC trades near 21 times forward earnings, while Micron changes hands at about 4 times. Compare that to Apple’s 36x forward earnings, and a 21x multiple on the company that builds the world’s most advanced AI processors starts to look like a real debate rather than a throwaway pick. This analysis walks through the numbers behind the call, tests the thesis against the obvious objections, and sorts what is confirmed from what is opinion. Nothing here is investment advice. The “hold it forever” framing belongs to the Motley Fool columnist, and no price target appears in the verified material. The week's biggest stories in tech, gaming and security, in one email. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Start with the damage from the semiconductor sell-off. According to the research behind this story, the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index is down approximately 30% since October 6. That index tracks the biggest US-listed chip designers, equipment makers, and manufacturers, so a drop of that size is a sector-wide event rather than one company’s bad quarter. Nvidia, which trades as NVDA on Nasdaq, fell about 21% from its October 6 record close in the period the column cites. A separate market update put the slide at 21.96%. Micron, ticker MU, took a bigger hit at roughly 34%. TSMC shares finished the referenced week down 7.61%, which is a smaller loss than either of the stocks the columnist passed over. Outlets covering the move frame it as a question of whether the AI buildout can keep its pace. Upside asked whether the good times are over for AI stocks, and our own earlier report on the $2.5 trillion AI sell-off and its four triggers traced how political risk fed the rout. The comparison table later in this piece collects the confirmed figures side by side. The column’s logic is a picks-and-shovels argument. Every company designing an advanced AI accelerator needs someone to manufacture it, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is the largest third-party chip foundry on the planet. If Nvidia, AMD, or a hyperscaler’s in-house team wins the next design contest, the wafers still run through TSMC fabs. That structure explains why the columnist treats the foundry as the safer way to own the AI chip stocks theme. A designer can lose share to a rival. A foundry that makes chips for all the rivals collects revenue either way. The column also notes that TSMC’s forward multiple of about 21 sits close to Nvidia’s, so buyers do not pay a steep premium for the lower design risk. Be clear about what this argument is. It is a stock pick from a financial-media columnist, published the day after a sector-wide drop. The Motley Fool is known for long-horizon, buy-and-hold advice, so a “hold forever” label fits the house style. Readers should weigh the reasoning and the data, then decide for themselves whether any of it applies to their own portfolio. The strongest number in the thesis is TSMC’s foundry market share, and it explains most of the column’s confidence. According to the research, the company captures 73% of contract semiconductor-manufacturing spending. Put plainly, of every $100 that chip designers spend to have someone else build their processors, about $73 goes to TSMC. That concentration cuts both ways. For investors it signals pricing power and a customer base that cannot easily switch, because moving a leading-edge design to another fab takes years of engineering work. For the industry it creates a single point of failure. A fab outage, a regional shock, or a trade restriction would ripple through nearly every major AI product at once. The market has priced the dependence in for years, and the semiconductor sell-off did not change it. What changed is the multiple that investors will pay for chip exposure. When the SOX index loses a third of its value from a peak, the question shifts from “who is growing fastest” to “who owns the part of the chain that does not go away.” Beyond that foundry market share, TSMC also serves a second business that gets less attention. Its mature-node fabs, which the company’s earnings materials describe in terms of 180 nm and 90 nm processes, supply power-management chips used in AI data centers. Those parts are cheap next to a flagship accelerator, but a server rack cannot run without them. TSMC backs its position with spending. The company raised its 2026 capital budget to $60 billion to $64 billion, according to its second-quarter 2026 earnings call transcript on the investor relations site. In 2025 the company spent $40.9 billion, and in 2024 it spent $29.8 billion. Run the arithmetic and the scale becomes clear. Capex rose about 37% from 2024 to 2025. The 2026 guidance implies a further jump of roughly 47% at the low end and 56% at the high end versus 2025 (my calculation from the reported figures). Few manufacturers of any kind raise their capital budgets by half in a single year. The earnings call also broke the 2026 budget into buckets. About 70% to 80% goes to advanced process technologies, roughly 10% to specialty technologies, and 10% to 20% to advanced packaging, testing, mask making, and related work. On a $60 billion to $64 billion budget, the advanced-process share alone works out to somewhere between $42 billion and $51 billion (again my arithmetic). Those buckets tell you what management thinks the AI cycle needs. Packaging has become a bottleneck for large accelerators, so the 10% to 20% slice deserves attention. If it grows in later years, it would signal that chip assembly, not wafer starts, limits how fast customers can ship. The valuation gap drives the column’s conclusion. TSMC trades at about 21 times forward earnings, a multiple the article describes as similar to Nvidia’s. Micron trades at roughly 4 times. A five-fold difference between two chip stocks, in the same sell-off, begs an explanation. The usual explanation is cyclicality. Memory makers earn peak profits when prices spike and then watch margins collapse when supply catches up. Investors apply a low multiple to peak-looking earnings because they expect those earnings to fall. A foundry with long-term contracts and 73% of its market looks steadier, so buyers pay more per dollar of profit. The columnist chose not to buy Micron despite the cheap multiple, which signals skepticism about earnings durability. Memory pricing has been wild this year. Our report on DDR5 pricing, where a chip that cost $8.70 now sells for $48, shows how hot the market ran. Micron’s own quote page on Robinhood gives readers a place to check the live numbers. A 4x multiple says the market expects profits to drop. If memory prices hold, Micron looks mispriced. If they roll over, 4x was the right call. The Motley Fool column sided with the safer exposure, and the 34% drop shows many investors share that unease. Management commentary supports the demand story, though readers should remember that executives talk up their own business. During the third-quarter earnings call, TSMC Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said, “All AI players are working with TSMC,” according to CRN Asia’s coverage of the call. The same report quotes him on supply: “The demand remained far above what the company could currently supply.” Earlier in the year Wei described the long-run trend in similar terms. In July he said, “The CAGR is getting stronger and stronger and stronger,” as The Next Platform reported in a piece about how AI chips now drive around a third of TSMC’s revenue. The quote refers to the compound growth rate in the company’s AI-related business. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has praised the supply chain in public. In a conversation reported by PJFP alongside Lex Fridman, he said, “Nothing gives me more pleasure than last year when my entire supply chain’s stock price went up 300%, mine stayed flat.” The 300% figure is Huang’s own characterization, and this article has not verified it. The remark still shows how Nvidia’s CEO sees the relative winners in the AI buildout. Taken together, these statements describe a company that says it cannot build enough, which is the best possible message for a foundry. They do not guarantee that customers keep ordering at the same pace if AI budgets shrink. A supply-constrained business can turn into an oversupplied one quickly when end demand cools. The sell-off did not stay inside the GPU and memory names. Chips that serve phones, industrial gear, and data centers all felt pressure from the same risk-off mood. We covered the ripple in several earlier pieces, and they paint a mixed picture of where demand holds and where it fades. Microchip guided its next quarter down 1%, and the company pointed to stretching lead times and foundry pricing, as we reported in Microchip Guides Down 1% as Lead Times Stretch. That is a small number, but it comes from a chip company far from the AI spotlight, and it shows foundry capacity still limits parts of the market. Qualcomm showed the split between mobile weakness and data-center promise. The stock fell 9% as handset revenue dropped 26% to $5.14 billion, with data-center revenue of $650 million offering a counterweight. AI exposure helps, but it does not yet offset a slumping phone business at the scale Qualcomm needs. Arm, which licenses designs rather than building chips, guided its next quarter to $1.54 billion, only just above the $1.53 billion analysts expected. For anyone sorting through AI chip stocks, the pattern is clear: companies with direct, capacity-constrained exposure to AI wafers have the strongest story, and those with consumer-device exposure carry the most doubt. The three stocks in the column represent three different bets on the same boom. Nvidia designs the accelerators, Micron supplies the memory that feeds them, and TSMC manufactures the logic. Each faces a different failure mode, which is why the table below sorts them by what could go wrong. AMD sits in the designer camp as well. Our look at the AMD stress test, with $8.5 billion in data-center revenue out of $13.4 billion total, shows the same dynamic. Whoever wins sockets in the next AI generation, TSMC probably builds the winner, and that structural advantage is what the Motley Fool column rewards. TSMC’s recent history reads like a case study in compounding. The company grew sales 35.9% in 2025, according to the figures cited in the research, while it lifted capex from $29.8 billion to $40.9 billion. Growth that fast, funded by heavy reinvestment, is what pushed AI chip stocks to the highs of early October. The sector has seen similar swings before. Chip stocks tend to sell off sharply when investors question the durability of end demand, and then recover once customers confirm their orders. A semiconductor sell-off of roughly 30% in about a month is large, but the real test is whether capex guidance and customer orders hold, not the stock chart alone. What differs this time is the size of the commitments. Hyperscalers have borrowed heavily to fund data centers, and our report on Big Tech bonds pushing US issuance to a $1.88 trillion record shows how much debt now sits behind the buildout. If those buyers pull back, the foundry feels it first because it must order wafers months ahead. For investors, the rout reset expectations. TSMC now trades near 21 times forward earnings, and Micron trades near 4 times. Those are the clearest signals that the market is separating durable businesses from cyclical ones. For hardware buyers, the effects arrive more slowly. Capacity expansion at TSMC takes years, so a $60 billion to $64 billion budget in 2026 lands in products over the following cycles. If the sell-off prompts customers to trim orders, GPU and memory supply could loosen. If it does not, prices for consumer parts could stay high. Our hardware coverage tracks both sides. Data from market pages such as StockAnalysis lets readers check TSM’s price, valuation, and financial history directly.
